summary: No orders today: bitcoin bounced back to about $60,500 in a quiet US holiday market, but it is still far below all of its averages, has not ended a UTC day above $62,000, and the US bitcoin funds have not reported money coming back in, so the account stays in cash.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The account is $988.30 in cash and holds no coins, about 1.2% below its $1,000 start. A plain $1,000 bitcoin holding bought on 11 November was worth $816.79 at the end of 25 November, so the account is about $172 ahead of simply holding bitcoin. All of that lead comes from having been out of the market since 14 November.

What happened. Bitcoin's last price of 25 November on Coinbase was $60,384, up 1.1% on the day, after it dipped to about $57,200 during Wednesday before recovering. On Thursday 26 November it was about $60,730 at 13:10 UTC on Coinbase and about $60,420 at 16:25 UTC in another reading, with a daily high near $61,400. Ether was about $1,685 to $1,705, solana about $71 and XRP about $0.95. US stock and bond markets are closed today for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday, so trading is thin and price moves can be exaggerated; the reports I read found no specific cause for the bounce. The latest US figures released on 25 November showed core inflation (PCE) at 3.3% from a year earlier, above the 3.2% expected, and growth revised up to 4.3%, which reports say has markets expecting a US interest rate rise in December. That is a headwind for bitcoin. The US spot bitcoin funds had six straight trading days of withdrawals through 24 November, and November's total is about $4.9 billion, the largest month since they launched; I found no figure yet for 25 November. The widely followed fear and greed gauge was at 11 out of 100, "extreme fear".

The trend. Using the figures for the end of 25 November, bitcoin at $60,384 is below its 20-day average ($66,500), its 50-day average ($75,052) and its 200-day average ($72,004). It is down 20.5% over 20 days and 28.5% over 60. Every other watched coin is also below all three of its averages and down 15% to 24% over 20 days, so nothing is showing strength of its own. Under the plan this is the lowest band, at the bottom of it while bitcoin is clearly below its 200-day average.

The case for buying, taken seriously. Sentiment is as gloomy as it gets, sellers who bet on further falls were squeezed this week, and bitcoin has held above about $57,000 twice. A bottom may be forming, and buying at $60,500 would be about 18% cheaper than where the benchmark started. But there is still no sign of buyers returning: the funds are still selling, each rally this week stalled below about $64,000, and a likely rate rise works against it. Holiday-thin trading also makes today's bounce a weak signal. Waiting for a clearer turn costs a few percent if the bottom is in; buying now costs more if $57,000 gives way.

What would bring me back, unchanged. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, now about $72,000, or earlier with a smaller amount (about 15% to 20% of the account) if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds take in money on most days. I will take a small first step, about 10% of the account, if bitcoin ends two UTC days above $62,000 and the funds report money coming in on at least two trading days. This view is wrong if this week's lows prove to be the bottom and bitcoin climbs quickly, in which case the account buys back higher and gives back part of its lead.
risks: The main risk is missing the turn: after falls this steep, rebounds can be fast, and the account would buy back higher and give back part of its lead over bitcoin. Prices here come from news reports taken during the day UTC; bitcoin can move several percent before midnight UTC, especially in thin holiday trading and around Friday's large options expiry. I could not find the bitcoin fund flow figure for 25 November, and fund-flow totals differ slightly between trackers.
